title: {{NAME}} and the Meadow Cup
moral: The best games are the ones where everyone belongs.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a meadow-green jersey with tiny silver stars, white shorts, and green-silver cleats — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
The Meadow Cup had no formal rules when {{NAME}} arrived to referee it.

It was played every midsummer in the large meadow between the town and Thornwood: humans, fairies, and occasionally a unicorn if one happened to be in the area.

This year, one happened to be.

The unicorn was named Wisp and she had been watching human football from the Thornwood for three summers and had, apparently, decided this was the year to participate.

{{NAME}} had never refereed a match with a unicorn before.

"What's the rule on horns?" someone asked.

"Working on it," said {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
He drafted the Meadow Cup Special Rules in twenty minutes, on a piece of paper leaned against a fence post.

Unicorn rules: horn may not touch the ball directly. No flight over opposing players. Must remain within the meadow boundary.

Fairy rules: no charms. Standard elevation limits.

Human rules: standard.

"This is the most creative rulebook I've ever seen," said the fairy captain.

"It's the only rulebook this match has ever had," said {{NAME}}. "You've been playing without rules for six years."

"It worked out," she said.

"This will work out better," he said.

pages.content:
The match was the most chaotic and joyful football {{NAME}} had ever seen.

Wisp could not use her horn but she could use her nose, which turned out to be an extraordinary ball-control implement, nudging passes at precise angles and trapping the ball with complete confidence.

The fairies, without charms, played their fastest and most skillful game.

The humans played as if they'd been freed from seriousness.

{{NAME}} refereed and forgot to whistle half the time because he was too busy watching.

"You're a terrible referee," said someone.

"Best match I've ever seen," said {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
There was no final score anyone agreed on.

Three different counters had three different numbers.

Everyone agreed: it didn't matter.

Wisp trotted over to {{NAME}} after the final whistle.

She touched her horn to his clipboard.

The handwritten rulebook glowed briefly.

"She's keeping it," said the fairy captain.

"The rules?"

"The memory of them. Unicorns remember the structure of fair things. She'll carry it."

pages.content:
He walked home through the meadow as the midsummer light faded.

The fairies had gone back to Thornwood. The humans had gone home. Wisp stood at the meadow's edge, horn faintly glowing, before walking into the trees.

{{NAME}} sat on the fence for a while and watched the meadow return to stillness.

Then he walked home and went to bed and fell asleep before he'd finished thinking the thought he'd started.

In the meadow, far away, Wisp moved through the Thornwood, carrying the shape of a fair game in her ancient memory.
